figures.caption: Figure 3: Median RMSE of CATE estimates comparing τ̂MAR (blue), τ̂MCCAR (orange), and τ̂Oracle (green) in the MAR (top) and MCCAR (bottom) settings over 500 iterations against the rate of noise (ϵ ∼ N(−n−α, n−2α)) added to all nuisance functions. In the MAR setting, τ̂MCCAR remains biased even after more treatments are observed, while in the MCCAR setting both estimators are unbiased and τ̂MAR achieves slightly faster convergence.

Figure 7: Median RMSE of CATE estimates comparing τ̂MAR (blue), τ̂MCCAR (orange), and τ̂Oracle (green) in the MAR (a) and MCCAR (b) settings over 500 iterations against the rate of noise added to all nuisance functions. In the MAR setting (top), τ̂MCCAR remains biased even after more treatments are observed, while in the MCCAR setting (bottom) both estimators are unbiased and τ̂MAR achieves slightly faster convergence. This pattern holds across all observation rates including 25% and 75%.

Figure 9: AUPEC with 95% confidence intervals, where zero indicates no gain over random policy. Results show average performance across treatment observation rates for STAR (10 iterations) and Voting (5 iterations) datasets under MAR and MCCAR missingness. Left: varying model initialization seed. Right: varying train-test split seed. Train-test split variation introduces substantially more uncertainty than model seed variation. The results support our main conclusions: in the MAR setting, DR-MAR outperforms all other estimators, while in the MCCAR setting all models are competitive. We omit MTRNET from this comparison due to computational costs.

Figure 4: Average RMSE of CATE estimates comparing τ̂MAR (blue), τ̂MCCAR (orange), τ̂Oracle (green), outcome (purple) and propensity-score (brown) models in the MAR and MCCAR settings with increasing sample size. In the MAR setting, τ̂MCCAR remains biased, while in the MCCAR setting both τ̂MCCAR and τ̂MAR converge to the oracle.

Figure 8: Average AUPEC of CATE estimators (zero is no gain over a random policy), averaged over 10 seeds (STAR) and 5 seeds (Voting) under MAR and MCCAR missingness. The DR-MAR estimator performs better in all settings. All models, except the risk model, perform well in the MCCAR setting.

Table 8: Policy values on the test set, averaged over 10 replications varying the missingness seed. Left columns show the percentage of treatments observed and the available treatment budget κ. Highest policy value in each row is in bold. Overall, DR-MAR has the most wins, but DR-CC and DR-MCCAR are also competitive in this setting.
Figure 13: Example policy values over different budgets and treatment observation rates. At treatment observation rates greater than 10%, all doubly-robust models are competitive.

Table 7: Policy values on the test set, averaged over 10 replications varying the missingness seed. Left columns show the percentage of treatments observed and the available treatment budget κ. Highest policy value in each row is in bold. DR-MAR outperforms all other methods at low treatment observation rates and achieves the highest overall average policy value.

Figure 12: Example policy values across budgets and treatment observation rates. Even at low treatment observation rates, DR-MAR achieves high policy values. All DR-methods perform well at high treatment observation rates.
Table 3: Hyperparameter grid for base learners

Figure 6: Average Area-Under-the-Prescriptive-EffectCurve (AUPEC) of CATE estimators (zero is no gain over a random policy), averaged over 10 seeds (STAR) and 5 seeds (Voting) under MAR and MCCAR missingness. In the MAR setting, DR-MAR and OR, which use imputation models for missing treatment data, outperform all other methods. Under MCCAR, most methods perform similarly.

Table 6: Policy values calculated from the test set, averaged over 5 iterations varying the missingness seed. Left columns show the percentage of treatments observed and the available treatment budget κ. Highest policy value in each row is in bold. DR-MAR, DR-CC, and DR-MCCAR all perform similarly, while MTRNET performs well at higher budgets even with treatment observation rates.
Figure 11: Example policy values over different budgets and treatment observation rates. In the MCCAR setting, all methods are competitive.

Table 5: Policy values on the test set, averaged over 5 iterations varying the missingness seed. Left columns show the percentage of treatments observed and the available treatment budget κ. Highest policy value in each row is in bold. DR-MAR outperforms all other methods at low treatment observation rates and is competitive with higher observation rates.

Figure 10: Example policy values across budgets and treatment observation rates. At low treatment observation rates, DR-MCCAR fails to use the entire treatment budget. DR-MAR outperforms other methods at low observation rates, with all methods converging at high observation rates

Figure 2: Asymptotic Relative Efficiency gains of φMAR over ϕMCCAR ( ARE(ϕMCCAR, φMAR) := Var(ϕMCCAR) Var(φMAR) ) as a function of the average of λd (left), the average of 1− π (center), and the correlation between λd and 1− π (right). When not varied, the average values of λd, 1− π, and their correlation are held fixed at 0.5. ARE increases with the augmented propensity score λd, missingness probability 1− π, and their correlation.
